How I Did It: Tunnel Hero

by Sal, Galaxy Zone Arcade

Sal remembers the original cabinet

Dig Dug showed up in '82, right in the thick of the good years, and it was the politest hit I ever had — no lasers, no explosions, just a little guy with a bicycle pump. There was a kid, Marcus, who figured out you got double points for popping the dragon sideways, and he guarded that secret like it was a bank code. Charged other kids a quarter to tell them. I let him, because honestly, it was good information.

What the remodel changed

The old '25 version was barely Dig Dug — you sort of wandered around collecting vegetables and mashing a button. Embarrassing, looking back. This time I asked for the whole machine: the pump that takes three squeezes, the dragons that pause and glow before they breathe fire — that pause is your warning, same as the cabinet — the monsters that go see-through and float at you right through the dirt, and the rocks. Oh, the rocks. Dig under one and it wobbles like it's deciding, then it comes down on whoever's dumb enough to still be standing there. Sometimes that's you. Everything moves smooth now too, on the fixed-clock business the whole remodel runs on, and digging actually feels slower than running through an open tunnel, the way it should.

The spell that did it

Rebuild Tunnel Hero properly this time. Four layers of dirt, darker and worth more the deeper you go. The pump takes three hits to pop a monster and they deflate if I stop pumping. Dragons telegraph before a two-square flame. Monsters should occasionally ghost through the dirt straight at me, more often the longer I stall. Rocks wobble and fall when I dig under them — crushing counts for 1000 — and after two rocks drop a bonus vegetable shows up. And give the dragon double points if I pop him sideways. A kid named Marcus will know why.

Under the hood

  • The dirt is a 20-wide grid under one strip of sky, split into four depth bands — 200, 300, 400, 500 points a pop depending on how deep you are when you do the popping.
  • Digging and walking use the same smooth tile-to-tile mover as the other maze games, but the speed drops when the square you're entering still has dirt in it. That little slowdown is what makes digging feel like digging.
  • The ghost trick is just the monster ignoring the grid: it drifts in a straight line toward me and only turns solid again when it's centered over an open tunnel square. Its urge to do this grows with a timer that shrinks as the level drags on.
  • A rock watches the square under itself every frame. Open square means wobble, wobble means fall, and a falling rock checks everything it passes through — monsters, me, no favorites — before it shatters at the bottom.
